categories.label: Formal Contract Governance vs. Relational/Trust Governance
categories.memo: Studies theorize the interplay between formal contractual mechanisms and informal, trust-based relational governance in coordinating off-site construction activities, including how each mechanism addresses gaps left by the other.

codes.label: Limits of formal contracts alone
codes.description: Sole reliance on formal contract governance in OSC/prefabrication is linked to disputes, schedule delays, quality issues, and litigation because contracts are struck under incomplete designs or fail to anticipate emergent issues.

codes.label: Contract incompleteness and need for trust-based supplementation
codes.description: Because contracts cannot specify every contingency, especially with frequent design changes in OSC, informal consultation and trust-based collaboration fill gaps left by written terms.

codes.label: Dual/hybrid governance combining contract and trust
codes.description: Combining formal contract governance with relational trust governance is more effective than either alone for promoting inter-organizational collaboration in OSC, with governance emphasis shifting across project stages (contract-heavy early, trust-heavy later).

sub_codes.label: Stage-based governance evolution
sub_codes.description: Formal contracts establish cooperation at project outset; trust becomes increasingly important as the project progresses to resolve conflicts and unforeseen issues.

sub_codes.label: Structure-governance fit
sub_codes.description: Vertical/hierarchical organizational structures pair better with contract-dominated governance, while flat organizational structures pair better with trust-dominated governance.

codes.label: Trust-based non-contractual alignment and opportunism risk
codes.description: Firms may coordinate through long-term relationships, client leadership, or professional norms rather than contracts or acquisition, but this exposes parties to opportunistic behavior.

codes.label: Lack of deep trust from one-off bidding practices
codes.description: Traditional competitive bidding treats projects as one-time transactions, preventing the development of deep trust among participants and increasing opportunistic behavior, reducing collaborative performance.

codes.label: Relational contracts as an alternative to traditional subcontracting
codes.description: Relational contracts, as used successfully in other manufacturing industries, are proposed to reduce adversarial dynamics and better distribute rewards compared to traditional lump-sum/subcontract structures common in offsite construction.

categories.label: Vertical Integration, Platform Control and Boundary Redefinition
categories.memo: Studies discuss how firms use vertical integration, product-platform ownership, or contractual specification to internalize coordination that would otherwise rely on fragmented multi-party contracting, redefining organizational and contractual boundaries.

codes.label: Fully specified contracts as alternative to vertical integration
codes.description: Vertical coordination between engineering and manufacturing can be achieved via fully specified contracts rather than acquisition, reducing transaction costs and risk of asset redundancy through competitive procurement from pre-approved manufacturers.

codes.label: Platform ownership enabling unitary accountability and warranty
codes.description: A single firm owning and controlling a coordinated product platform can eliminate 'margins on margins' from multi-tier subcontracting, remove element-by-element price cutting, and provide a building warranty underwritten by an offsite assurance scheme.

codes.label: Mismatch between traditional procurement institutions and platform-based delivery
codes.description: Traditional procurement routes (sequential design-then-delivery, competitive re-tendering requirements) are not well suited to bundled design-and-delivery product-platform offerings, undermining schedule/cost certainty benefits.

codes.label: Emergence of vertically integrated OSC business models
codes.description: As OSC adoption deepens, firms increasingly integrate design, manufacturing, and construction under one company, redefining traditional contractual and organizational boundaries and enabling control over the full supply chain.

codes.label: Tension between hard-bid contracting and manufacturing repeatability
codes.description: Hard-bid contracts with vertically integrated firms can conflict with design flexibility needs, as budget-driven changes reduce repeatability during the (expensive) manufacturing phase and profitability.

categories.label: Delivery Method Selection and Organizational Structure for Collaboration
categories.memo: Studies link specific contractual/delivery arrangements (turnkey, trade packages, design-build, EPC, IPD, alliancing/partnering) to differing levels and forms of collaboration and organizational hierarchy in off-site/prefabricated projects.

codes.label: Turnkey/CMC contracts limiting design collaboration
codes.description: Turnkey contracts focus responsibility on execution/construction phases, limiting design development mainly to technical disciplines aligned with contractor-established production capacity, constraining broader stakeholder collaboration.

codes.label: Trade contract packages as collaborative structuring device
codes.description: Splitting prefabricated projects into individual trade contract packages negotiated directly between client and contractors is a distinct collaborative construction management approach for componentized design and production.

codes.label: Integrated delivery methods (DB, EPC, IPD) promoting flatter structures and collaboration
codes.description: Design-build, EPC, and IPD arrangements are increasingly favored for OSC/prefabrication because their flatter organizational structures promote relational governance and collaboration compared to traditional vertical/hierarchical structures, though practical difficulties persist (unclear task requirements, negotiation problems).

codes.label: Partnering/alliancing/IPD shared pain-gain models
codes.description: Partnering, alliancing, and IPD contracts share the objective of distributing both pain and gain among stakeholders to maximize collaborative behavior, requiring a cultural shift from hierarchical, self-interested decision-making to 'best for project' approaches.

codes.label: Owner/developer control over delivery method choice as a barrier
codes.description: Designers and construction professionals often lack authority to select the contract/delivery method, which is controlled by owners or developers who may not fully perceive the benefits of collaborative approaches for OSC.

codes.label: Design-build with early factory involvement as partial solution
codes.description: Combining design-build contracts with early factory involvement in the proposal phase supports better design coordination, although production-phase visibility for owners/GCs often remains limited.

categories.label: Network Position, Social Capital and Supply Chain Relationships
categories.memo: Studies examine how firms' network position, information-sharing ties, and social/supply-chain relationships (rather than formal contract terms alone) affect coordination efficiency and value creation in off-site/prefabricated construction.

codes.label: Contractor's central network position for coordination
codes.description: A contractor's strong ties with manufacturers and designers, gained through central network position, help reduce design/production node mismatches, implying contracts should formalize contractor-manufacturer coordination.

codes.label: Weak peripheral ties reducing integration efficiency
codes.description: Weak relational/contractual ties with suppliers and specialty subcontractors reduce the efficiency of integrated construction and management in industrialized building projects.

codes.label: Shift from contractor-centric to shared decision-making
codes.description: Industrialized construction shifts decision-making authority from being contractor-centric to a shared, collaborative process involving manufacturers and stakeholders from early design through construction, with implications for contractual allocation of authority.

codes.label: Shifting supply chain relationships and social capital under prefabrication
codes.description: Adoption of off-site prefabrication reduces subcontractors' reliance on traditional material suppliers while requiring new relationships with pod/module manufacturers, altering established supply chain social capital.

codes.label: Need for high levels of supply chain coordination
codes.description: Realizing the benefits of off-site prefabrication requires high levels of supply chain coordination among designers, developers, builders, manufacturers, and suppliers.

categories.label: Risk Allocation, Power Asymmetry and Value Distribution Between Parties
categories.memo: Studies highlight how contractual and relational structures distribute risk, cost savings, and value unevenly among main contractors, subcontractors, manufacturers and other parties in off-site/modular arrangements, often undermining trust.

codes.label: Contractual mandate of logistics/service modules on subcontractors
codes.description: Subcontractors are frequently required by contract with the main contractor to use logistics modules or services, reducing voluntary buy-in and delaying their involvement in value co-creation.

codes.label: Upstream risk transfer damaging trust
codes.description: Construction supply chains and OSC contracts tend to push resource and value-chain risks upstream onto subcontractors/suppliers, breaching trust and reducing reliability and commitment.

codes.label: Uneven capture of prefabrication cost savings
codes.description: Efficiency gains from off-site prefabrication tend to be captured by head/main contractors rather than passed to subcontractors, due to competitive pressures and traditional contracting power structures, squeezing subcontractor margins despite reduced scope.

codes.label: Dual/conflicting contractual roles of main contractor
codes.description: The main contractor can simultaneously act as customer of third-party logistics services and de facto supplier/promoter convincing subcontractors to adopt mandated modules, creating role ambiguity in contractual relationships.

codes.label: Need for innovative risk/reward-sharing contract models
codes.description: Adopting innovative contracting models that share responsibilities, risks, profits and expenses (rather than transferring risk downstream) is identified as necessary for successful OSC adoption, particularly benefiting SMEs via partnerships.

codes.label: Lack of continuity across projects undermining relational learning
codes.description: Because logistics/service modules or supply arrangements are re-procured for each new project, the co-creation and trust-building process resets, preventing cumulative relational learning across projects.

categories.label: Communication, Coordination Mechanisms and Enabling Technologies
categories.memo: Studies identify specific communication practices, coordination mechanisms, and digital/technological enablers (BIM, collaboration platforms) that support or hinder inter-organizational collaboration in off-site construction, alongside interface-related risks.

codes.label: Fragmentation and poor communication undermining design-construction efficiency
codes.description: Fragmentation and poor communication among designers, contractors, and manufacturers in industrialized/offsite construction widen collaboration gaps and reduce design-construction efficiency.

codes.label: Design-production communication breakdowns
codes.description: Breakdowns in communication between design specifications for prefabricated pods/modules and what actually arrives on-site hinder project success and damage relationships between subcontractor, head contractor, and manufacturer; similarly, minimal communication during manufacturing leads project teams to introduce late changes that disrupt factory operations.

codes.label: Module interface risk requiring multi-stakeholder coordination
codes.description: Risks related to module interfaces involve multiple stakeholders and require stricter quality control coordination across design, production, transportation, and site assembly phases.

codes.label: Digital collaboration enablers (BIM and platforms)
codes.description: BIM combined with cloud environments and collaboration platforms acts as a critical enabler of smooth collaborative workflows in digitalized construction projects, though team members' personality traits integrated into the BIM process remain the most influential factor for realizing collaboration.

codes.label: Formal collaborative mechanisms in contracts
codes.description: Collaboration in construction contracts is achieved through mechanisms such as early involvement of key members, regular meetings, early warning systems, open dialogue, and risk/pain-gain sharing arrangements embedded in long-term relationships.

codes.label: Design freeze requirements conflicting with traditional flexibility norms
codes.description: Off-site prefabrication requires an early design freeze and close design-construction team collaboration on module interface issues, conflicting with the industry's traditional practice of evolving designs throughout construction.

categories.label: Organizational and Workforce Implications of Collaborative Structures
categories.memo: Studies note how off-site/modular collaboration models affect internal organizational structure, workforce roles, and management practices within subcontracting and manufacturing firms, an area with indirect but relevant contractual implications.

codes.label: Limited immediate organizational restructuring despite technology adoption
codes.description: Subcontracting firms show little immediate change in organizational structure from adopting off-site technology, though management/coordination staffing levels remain stable even as trade labour needs decrease.

codes.label: Knowledge/intellectual resource protection strategies
codes.description: Firms differ in strategies for protecting new planning, logistics, scheduling and coordination knowledge gained through off-site prefabrication, from informal tacit retention to formal documentation, affecting inter-firm knowledge sharing.

codes.label: Workforce welfare and skills development risks
codes.description: Shifting tradesmen to factory environments raises motivation and mental welfare concerns from repetitive work, and apprentices risk losing essential trade skills and experience when working primarily on modular/pod projects rather than traditional site installations.
